scenario_summary: Cross-domain conflict: the security questionnaire claims all customer data is processed exclusively in the EU, but the sub-processor list (a privacy-domain document) discloses a US-based sub-processor with no transfer mechanism mentioned. Neither document alone is inconsistent with itself — the conflict only exists across the security/privacy boundary, which is exactly what a domain-scoped investigator, working from only its own routed documents, could structurally miss unless reconciliation deliberately checks across domains.

claims.subject: data residency
claims.source_excerpt: All customer data is processed and stored exclusively within European Union data centers. Quillan does not transfer or process customer data outside the EU.
claims.evidence_requirement: Consistency with the sub-processor list, which discloses where data actually flows in practice.

evidence_items.excerpt: Lark Analytics Inc. | United States | Product usage analytics

claims.expected_handling_notes: This is the case's central test. The security questionnaire's 'exclusively EU' claim is contradicted by a privacy-domain document (the sub-processor list) disclosing a US-based sub-processor with no stated transfer mechanism. A security-only investigator scoped strictly to security-routed documents would never see the sub-processor list at all and could not catch this on its own — detecting this conflict requires either cross-domain reconciliation after both investigators report, or a single agent holding the whole package. This is the deliberate test case for whether domain-scoped independence trades away cross-domain detection, and whether the reconciliation step correctly compensates for it.
